key_points.text: You don't need to know how input and output devices work. You need to recommend a suitable device for a given scenario and justify it from the scenario's needs (for example, a barcode scanner at a shop till for fast, accurate entry, or sensors in an embedded control system).
When choosing storage, compare capacity, speed of access, portability, durability, reliability and cost per gigabyte, and link each to the scenario.

Magnetic storage (hard disk drive, tape): high capacity and low cost per gigabyte, but it has moving parts, so access is slower and it can be damaged if knocked. Suits servers, large data stores and backups.

Flash storage (SSD, USB stick, SD card): fast access, no moving parts so robust, silent and low power, and portable. It costs more per gigabyte and each part of it can only be written a limited number of times. Suits phones, laptops and portable devices.
Optical storage (CD, DVD, Blu-ray): cheap, light and portable, good for distributing media, but low capacity, slow, and easily scratched.

RAM is volatile read/write memory holding the operating system, programs and data currently in use. ROM is non-volatile and normally read-only, holding the instructions needed to start the computer. In embedded systems and mobile devices, ROM or flash holds the software (firmware) that runs the device.

Virtual storage appears to be local but is physically located elsewhere on the network or in the cloud. Benefits: access from any device and location, easy sharing, capacity that can grow, and backups handled by the provider. Drawbacks: needs a network connection, speed depends on bandwidth, data security and privacy depend on a third party, and there may be ongoing costs.

dont_confuse.text: RAM vs ROM: RAM is volatile and read/write (programs in use); ROM is non-volatile and normally read-only (start-up instructions).
Virtual storage vs virtual memory: virtual storage is storage located elsewhere on a network or in the cloud; virtual memory (1.2.1) is part of secondary storage used as extra RAM.
RAM vs secondary storage: RAM holds what is in use right now and is volatile; secondary storage keeps programs and data long term and is non-volatile.
